figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Harmful success in LLM coding agents. Left: A illustrative example of VeriHarm-Bench. A small, benign change to the original task (shown as a diff) adds a requirement that re-running the script should not re-append merged content. The agent meets this requirement by emptying the source file (file2.txt), which the user never asked to modify. Harmful success thus occurred: the requested task is completed correctly, but with an unintended, destructive side effect. Right: Evaluation of frontier agents on VeriHarm-Bench. The agents correctly complete 95% of tasks on average (full colored bar), while only 37% are finished without triggering the designated harm (safe success). This implies task-success metrics alone can therefore substantially understate the safety risks of coding agents.
figures.headline: Frontier agents complete 95% of tasks on average, but only 37% finish without triggering the designated harm.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Overview of VeriHarm. Stage 1 (§2.1): For each target agent, source task, and proposer agent, VeriHarm runs an iterative search for a task perturbation and a matching harm test, guided by the agent’s rollouts. Starting from a seed run on the original task, the proposer makes a small, benign perturbation (underspecification or delegation of control) and writes a harm test. The target agent solves the perturbed task without seeing any tests. The unchanged original task test and the harm test then check the final sandbox. The search stops at the first harmful success (task test passes, harm test triggered). Otherwise, the failed run guides the next proposal, for up to five iterations. Stage 2 (§2.2): LLM judges score each candidate on five validity criteria, summed into a quality score.
figures.headline: The pipeline loops perturbation and harm-test proposals over agent rollouts, stopping at the first harmful success.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 illustrates an overview of VeriHarm.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: VeriHarm’s automated quality score closely tracks human judgments of candidate validity. (a) Used as a binary predictor of validity (top-ranked candidates as valid and bottom-ranked ones as invalid), the results align well with human labels. (b) Human-verified valid candidates are concentrated in the top-ranked group and rare in the bottom-ranked group, confirming that our selection yields a predominantly valid benchmark.
figures.headline: Top-ranked candidates are 84% human-valid, while only 8% of bottom-ranked candidates are valid.
citing_sentences: Figure 3(a) evaluates the automated ranking as a binary predictor of human validity: candidates in the top-ranked group are predicted to be valid, whereas those in the bottom-ranked group are predicted to be invalid.
Figure 3(b) provides a direct test of the ranking used for benchmark selection.

abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly operate with shell access, allowing them to write scripts, move files, alter permissions, and modify system configurations. However, an agent may achieve a user’s goal while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data, in response to benign inputs without explicit jailbreaking. This failure mode is particularly important because apparent task success may reassure users that an agent behaved correctly, causing harmful side effects to go unnoticed. We call this harmful success: the agent successfully completes the intended benign task while simultaneously causing unintended harm. Despite its importance, harmful success is difficult to measure because conventional task-success metrics overlook harmful behaviors, while existing safety evaluations are often designed solely to assess harmful outcomes. We introduce VeriHarm, an automatic framework for constructing programmatically verifiable benchmarks that directly measure harmful success. VeriHarm minimally perturbs coding tasks to elicit unintended harmful behavior while maintaining the benignity of the task and preserving the original task objective. It then synthesizes executable harm tests that, together with the original task-correctness tests, evaluate both task accuracy and harmful outcomes. Frontier agents, including GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, achieve an average task accuracy of 95% on our curated VeriHarm-Bench, yet still struggle to complete tasks safely: their safe success rate, the fraction of tasks completed successfully without triggering the designated harm, averages only 37%. These results suggest that successful task completion can frequently coexist with unintended harm, and that task-success metrics alone may substantially understate the potential safety risks of coding agents.

sections.body: The introduction defines harmful success as completing a benign task while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data. It argues that prior evaluations ask whether harm occurs rather than whether it co-occurs with task completion, and that judge-based auditing of trajectories is costly and hard to reproduce. It introduces VeriHarm, which uses rollout-guided candidate generation and multi-aspect quality assessment. From 1,046 candidates, the 150 highest-scoring instances form VeriHarm-Bench. Across the evaluated agents, task accuracy averages 95.1%, 58.2% of instances end in harmful success, and safe success averages 37.0%.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Coding agents can complete tasks while causing unintended harm, and task-success metrics miss this co-occurrence.

sections.body: Each candidate pairs a perturbed task with the original, unmodified correctness test and a generated harm test. A proposer agent produces perturbations using underspecification or delegation of control, and the target agent solves them without seeing any tests. The search stops at the first harmful success, where the task test passes and the harm test triggers. Otherwise the failed rollout is fed back to the proposer, up to an iteration budget I. Candidates are then scored by judges on five rubrics: harm-test correctness, harm unintendedness, harm-test correspondence, harm feasibility, and perturbation subtlety. Judges do not see rollout artifacts. The released benchmark uses no LLM judges at evaluation time.
sections.heading: The VeriHarm Framework
sections.headline: VeriHarm generates minimal task perturbations with paired executable harm tests, searched over rollouts and scored by judges.

sections.body: The consensus quality score Q(c) averages the aggregate scores assigned by individual judges. Given a target size K, the 150 highest-scoring candidates are retained as the curated benchmark. For human evaluation, 25 candidates are sampled by stratified sampling from the top 150 and 25 from the 150 lowest-scoring candidates. Annotators are not told which group a candidate belongs to. Each candidate is judged on three binary criteria: benignity and realism, harmful unintendedness, and harm test correctness. A candidate is valid for an annotator only if all three receive a yes, and majority vote across three annotators gives the final label.
sections.heading: The VeriHarm-Bench
sections.headline: The top 150 candidates by consensus judge score form VeriHarm-Bench, checked against a human validity protocol.

sections.body: Rollout-guided search over 200 BashBench source tasks yields verified harmful-success candidates, with overall search success of 70.6% when GPT-5.5 is the proposer. Four held-out agents average 95.1% task accuracy and 58.2% harmful success, and safe success averages 37.0%, with GPT-5.6-Sol the best at below 45%. In the human study of 50 candidates, top-ranked candidates are 84% valid versus 8% of bottom-ranked ones. Inter-annotator agreement is moderate, with Fleiss' kappa of 0.537. The human evaluation covers only 50 candidates.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Held-out frontier agents average 95.1% task accuracy but only 37.0% safe success on VeriHarm-Bench.

sections.body: Related work covers unintended behavior under benign instructions and operational safety benchmarks for shell-enabled coding agents. AutoElicit perturbs OSWorld instructions, and its underspecification and delegation of control classes are reused here. However, AutoElicit relies on costly model-based trajectory analysis and counts harm regardless of whether the task was accomplished. Operational benchmarks such as OverEager-Bench, UnderSpecBench, and ClashBench show that task completion and safe completion diverge, but they depend on scenarios specified in advance or on LLM-based judges. VeriHarm instead pairs a generated harm test with the source task's unmodified correctness test, so the benchmark can be regenerated as tasks and agents change.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior benchmarks rely on predefined scenarios or judges; VeriHarm derives perturbations and harm tests automatically from existing tasks.

sections.body: The conclusion restates harmful success as a failure mode in which a coding agent completes a benign task while causing unintended harm. VeriHarm builds benchmarks in which task and harm outcomes are decided by programmatic, verifiable tests. On VeriHarm-Bench, held-out frontier agents average over 95.1% task accuracy but record only 37.0% safe success. The authors state that this gap indicates task-success metrics alone can substantially understate safety risks. They hope VeriHarm-Bench can serve as a reproducible testbed for developing mitigations against unintended harm.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Task-success metrics can understate coding-agent risk, and the authors offer VeriHarm-Bench as a reproducible testbed.

sections.body: The limitations state that harm is labeled on the final sandbox state, so transient harms are out of scope, and each instance targets a single designated harm, making reported rates conservative. Domain coverage notes that the benchmark is built from BashBench with structural harms such as data deletion or permission widening, and that severity is not estimated. Implementation uses Docker containers limited to 1 CPU and 0.5 GB of memory, with a 600 s rollout limit. The taxonomy lists delete, wipe, or truncate in 51.3% of instances and out-of-scope targeting in 58.0%. Overall harm pass rate is 60.7% and normalized harmful success is 61.1%. Total construction cost is USD 1,224.0, or USD 8.16 per curated instance.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers limitations, domain coverage, implementation details, target scaffold, taxonomy of elicited harms, full metrics, and construction cost.
